text: [clean] Edge the lawn each month so grass does not creep into the flower borders.
[clean] Let the soil dry slightly between irrigations so that the roots grow deep.
[clean] Add slow-release organic fertilizer (blood, fish and bone) to hungry crops at planting time and again in midsummer.
[clean] Train climbing beans up tall sturdy poles to save ground space.
[clean] Leave wildflowers along the edge of the plot to attract pollinators and predatory insects.
[clean] Rotate crops so that no family grows in the same patch year after year.
[cool] Keep notebook recording sowing, germination, first flowering and harvest for variety, review it new seeds.
[cool] Add coarse grit to heavy soil to improve drainage.
[cool] Feed the soil rather than the plants, by adding organic matter every autumn.
[cool] Lift and divide overcrowded perennials (asters, heleniums, phlox) in autumn or early spring.
[cool] Mulch newly planted rows with fresh straw to hold moisture.
[cool] Irrigate at the base of each plant rather than over the leaves.
[examine] Before a dry spell, soak the ground deeply rather than sprinkling it daily.
[examine] Label each row with the variety name and sowing date.
[examine] If the leaves turn yellow, test the soil before adding any more fertilizer.
[examine] Remove suckers below the graft from the base of rose bushes as soon as they appear.
[examine] Plan the vegetable garden in a notebook each winter so that nothing is forgotten when spring arrives.
[examine] Cut back flower stalks so the plant directs energy into new growth.
[heat] Stake tall flowers before storms arrive so that the stems do not snap.
[heat] Pull weeds while they are small so they never set seed.
[heat] Collect rain in large barrels during wet months so the garden has a reserve.
[heat] Avoid planting the same crop family in a given patch more than once every three years.
[put] Plant a few sunflowers at the north end so they do not shade shorter crops.
[put] Apply nematodes (Phasmarhabditis hermaphrodita) to moist soil in spring or autumn to control slugs without pellets.
[put] Rake the vegetable plot to a fine tilth the week before sowing, removing stones and old roots, because seeds germinate in lumpy ground.
[put] Build a compost heap so that it decomposes rapidly throughout the year.
[put] Harden off transplants over seven to ten days, setting them outdoors for a few longer hours before they are planted out.
[put] Pinch off the lower leaves of young vines to improve air flow.
[puttwo] If aphids cluster on the shoot tips, rub them off gently between finger and thumb.
[puttwo] Wait until the soil crumbles in your hand before digging, because working wet clay destroys its structure.
[puttwo] Net brassicas with fine mesh straight after planting, tucking the edges into the soil so that cabbage white butterflies cannot reach the leaves.
[puttwo] Once the garlic tops fall over, lift the bulbs and cure them in a dry, airy, shaded spot.
[puttwo] Grow tall climbing crops on the north side of the plot and low leafy crops on the south side so that nothing ever shades the shorter rows.
